docs.title: zotero-backup
docs.text:
Backup and restore of Zotero libraries (personal library and groups) through the Zotero web API, keeping the item keys, so restored items are the same items: citations in Word, LibreOffice and Google Docs keep working.

  • Complete backups. Every backup is a folder with the whole library: items (with notes, annotations and the trash), collections, saved searches, library settings such as tag colours, the full-text index, and the attachment files.
  • Small and fast after the first run. Files that did not change since the previous backup are hard links to it: not downloaded again, not stored twice.
  • Restore into the same library, everything or selected items, with a preview first.
  • Look into backups without restoring (find, show, diff of two backups), schedule the daily backup with one command, and update zotero-backup itself (upgrade, signed).
  • One executable for Windows, macOS and Linux; nothing else to install.

Platform status: tested on macOS

zotero-backup is used and checked by hand on macOS, including the end-to-end stress test against Zotero desktop. The Windows and Linux versions are built for every release and pass all unit tests in CI on those systems, including the keychains, but have not yet been tried on a real Windows or Linux system: see #15 (Windows) and #16 (Linux). Reports are welcome.

The plan and the tests behind the design are in Issue #1.

Citing: zotero-backup is archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24090287 (all versions; each release has its own DOI there).

No warranty: you are responsible for your data

zotero-backup comes as it is, without any warranty. Nobody guarantees that a backup is complete or that a restore brings a library back as it was. restore writes into your Zotero library and prune deletes backups: look at what they will do first (diff, --dry-run), and keep other, independent copies of libraries that matter. Read the disclaimer.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Create an API key at https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys. For backups, a read-only key is enough: allow library access and notes for the personal library, and read access to the groups. For restores, create a second, read/write key (step 3): store both (two keys). Store it in the system keychain:

    # asks for the key (not shown), checks it with Zotero, stores it
zotero-backup key set
# the key's user, its libraries and what it may do in each
zotero-backup key check

    On a server without a keychain, set ZOTERO_API_KEY instead (Keys).

  2. Back up and look at what is there:

    # all libraries the key can read, into ~/zotero-backups
zotero-backup backup
zotero-backup list

  3. Restore needs a second key with write access, used only for restores:

    zotero-backup key set zotero-write
# what differs from the library today
zotero-backup diff ~/zotero-backups/group-<id>-<name>
# what restore would do (without --dry-run: shows the plan, asks, restores)
zotero-backup restore ~/zotero-backups/group-<id>-<name> --key zotero-write --dry-run

    With "write_key": "zotero-write" in the configuration, restore uses it without --key.

  4. Clean up old backups (keeps the newest of each of the last 7 days, 5 weeks and 12 months):

    zotero-backup prune --dry-run

First install it; more about keys, backups and restore.

AI assistants: skills/zotero-backup/SKILL.md is an Agent Skill that tells an assistant (e.g. Claude Code) how to use zotero-backup safely: keys only typed by you, a preview and your yes before every restore and prune. For Claude Code, copy the folder skills/zotero-backup into ~/.claude/skills/.

Contributing: reports, tests on Windows and Linux, and pull requests are welcome, see CONTRIBUTING.md; security problems are reported privately, see SECURITY.md. What changed per version: CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• Linked files (only the link is on the Zotero server).
  • What exists only in the Zotero app: feeds, plugins, styles, preferences. Copy the Zotero data folder for that.
  • Restoring into a different library, e.g. a new group after a group was deleted: citations link to the old library; planned in Issue #11.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
~/zotero-backups/
  group-2333076-IPBES_LDR/
    2026-11-05T190523Z/
      meta.json          library version, counts, files missing on the server, problems
      items.json  collections.json  searches.json  settings.json  fulltext.json
      files.json         attachment key → file name, md5, size
      files/<attachment key>/<file name>       (or <file name>.zip, see below)
    2026-11-06T060000Z/  …complete as well
  user-12022430-Rainer_M_Krug/
  • Folder names are group-<id>-<name> and user-<id>-<username> (spaces as _). A renamed group keeps its folder: it is found by ID and renamed.
  • Backup names are the time in UTC (YYYY-MM-DDTHHMMSSZ, no colons so they work on Windows), independent of the computer's time zone and of summer time; they sort by time.
  • Text files and web-page snapshots are kept as <file name>.zip: Zotero desktop uploads them zipped (a snapshot with its images and styles) and the server hands out that ZIP. Unzip it to open the file; restore uploads the ZIP the way Zotero does.
  • A file that did not change since the previous backup (same md5) is a hard link: deleting a backup frees only the files no other backup links to. On drives without hard links (FAT/exFAT, some network shares) files are copied instead. Never edit files inside a backup: a hard-linked file is the same file in every backup. Copy a backup folder tree with a tool that keeps hard links (e.g. rsync -aH), or each backup becomes a full copy: see Off-site copies.
  • An interrupted backup leaves <date>.partial; the next run continues it.
  • One run per library at a time. While a backup or prune works on a library, its folder holds a .lock file (process ID, computer, program, start time, command). A second run that finds it skips that library with "a backup of … is already running (PID …)" and counts it as failed (exit status 1, a notification if set up); the other libraries go on. A lock left by a run that no longer runs on this computer (a crash, a power cut) is taken over by the next run, with a warning; a lock from another computer (a backup folder on a shared disk) never is: the message says which file to remove once no backup runs there.
  • Attachments whose file never reached the Zotero server cannot be backed up; they are listed in meta.json and by backup, so they can be uploaded from the computer that has them.

docs.title: Running and stopping
docs.text:
zotero-backup status                 # the backups running now: library, PID, computer, since, command
zotero-backup stop                   # stop every backup running on this computer in the backup folder
zotero-backup stop group:2333076     # only the one of that library (or: stop user)

stop asks the run to stop as Ctrl-C would and waits until it has ended: the finished libraries stay complete, the unfinished one stays as <date>.partial for the next run, and its lock is removed. It only stops a process that really is the zotero-backup run of the lock, and never a run on another computer. (On Windows the run is ended hard; its .partial is continued all the same.)

docs.title: Looking into a backup
docs.text:
Without restoring anything, and without the network or an API key:

zotero-backup find "one health"                  # all libraries below the backup folder
zotero-backup find kruger ~/zotero-backups/group-6719916-Safe_Edit_Test
zotero-backup show ~/zotero-backups/group-6719916-Safe_Edit_Test 9FCKFFL3
zotero-backup show ~/zotero-backups/group-6719916-Safe_Edit_Test/2026-11-05T204338Z 9FCKFFL3 --save ~/Desktop/old
  • find TEXT searches every backup for items whose title, creators, DOI, key, note or annotation text or file name contains TEXT (upper and lower case alike). For each item it shows its key and title (from the newest backup that has it), its parent for notes and attachments, and in which backups it is: how many, the first and the last, and whether it is not in the newest backup (deleted since) or in the trash there. That is the way to find the backup to restore an item from.
  • show BACKUP KEY prints the item from that backup (BACKUP is a backup folder, or a library folder for its newest backup): its fields, creators, tags and collections, then its attachments, notes (as text) and annotations.

  • --save DIR copies the files of the item and its attachments out of the backup into DIR/<attachment key>/, ZIPs unpacked. It never overwrites a file and refuses a folder inside the backups.

  • diff BACKUP1 BACKUP2 compares two backups of the same library: what was added, removed and changed (with the fields) between them, files changed and settings changed. The order does not matter; parts either backup left out are not compared.

    zotero-backup diff ~/zotero-backups/group-6719916-Safe_Edit_Test/2026-11-05T204338Z ~/zotero-backups/group-6719916-Safe_Edit_Test/2026-11-10T102736Z

To put an item back into the library: zotero-backup restore BACKUP --items KEY (Restore).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A JSON file, by default in the user configuration folder (~/Library/Application Support/zotero-backup/config.json on macOS, ~/.config/zotero-backup/config.json on Linux, %AppData%\zotero-backup\config.json on Windows), or given with --config. Without a file, the defaults apply. zotero-backup config prints the configuration in effect, with every option.

Profiles are chosen with --profile NAME (default: default). Options a profile leaves out keep their default:

{
  "profiles": {
    "default": {
      "library": "all",
      "key": "zotero-backup",
      "to": "~/zotero-backups",
      "exclude": [],
      "write_key": "",
      "keep_daily": 7,
      "keep_weekly": 5,
      "keep_monthly": 12,
      "progress": "auto",
      "progress_interval": 30
    },
    "ldr": { "library": "group:2333076", "key": "zotero-readonly" },
    "mine": {
      "key": "readonly",
      "write_key": "zotero-write",
      "keys": { "group:6719916": "safe-edit-write", "user": "personal" }
    }
  }
}
Option Meaning library all (the personal library and every group the key can read), user, or group:<id> key name of the keychain entry holding the API key (the default key) keys per library, a different keychain entry: "user", "group:<id>" or "default" → name. With library: all, the default key lists the libraries; a library listed here is read with its own key, also if the default key cannot read it. diff and restore use the key for the backup's library, so a write key can be kept for the libraries that need restores. --key NAME uses one entry for everything in a run write_key keychain entry restore uses for every library (e.g. a key with write access), while backup and diff keep the read-only key / keys; empty: restore uses the library's key to folder for the backups exclude parts to leave out of backup and restore: files (records kept, file contents skipped), attachments, notes, annotations, fulltext, settings, trash; --exclude a,b overrides it for one run keep_daily, keep_weekly, keep_monthly prune keeps the newest backup of each of the last N days, ISO weeks and months (three generations); the newest backup is always kept progress auto (an updating line on a terminal, plain lines otherwise), line, log or quiet; --progress / --quiet override it progress_interval seconds between progress lines in log mode notify_command a program with its arguments, run after a backup that failed or reported problems, e.g. ["/usr/bin/mail", "-s", "zotero-backup", "me@example.org"]; no shell. It gets the backup's summary on stdin and ZB_STATUS (failed or problems) and ZB_LIBRARIES_FAILED in its environment, never an API key. See Scheduled backups notify_macos true: also a macOS notification then

Unknown options and invalid values are errors, so a typo does not go unnoticed.

docs.title: No warranty
docs.text: zotero-backup is provided "as is", without warranty of any kind, express or implied (see the MIT licence). Nobody guarantees that it works correctly, that a backup is complete, or that a restore brings a library back as it was. The authors are not liable for any loss or damage, including lost or changed Zotero data.

docs.title: Your responsibility
docs.text:
You use zotero-backup at your own risk and you are responsible for your data:

  • restore writes into a Zotero library: it creates, changes and trashes items, collections, searches, files and settings. Look at what it will do first with zotero-backup diff and zotero-backup restore --dry-run.
  • prune deletes backups. Check with zotero-backup prune --dry-run.
  • Keep other, independent copies of libraries that matter, for example a copy of the Zotero data folder or an export, and try a restore on a test group before you rely on it.
  • Sync every Zotero app that works on a library before restoring it (see Restore).
  • Check your backups: read the summary and meta.json of each backup for missing files and problems.
  • The stress test changes the libraries it runs on. Run it only on test groups or libraries, ideally of a separate Zotero account (see Stress test).
  • Keep your API keys safe. A key with write access can change every library it is allowed to write to.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install v0.3.0 (the first release that can update itself), then let it bring itself to the newest release. The commands stay the same for every future release, and the update is checked with zotero-backup's signature.

macOS and Linux, in Terminal. SYS is your system: uname -sm prints e.g. Darwin arm64 (→ darwin-arm64), Darwin x86_64 (→ darwin-amd64), Linux x86_64 (→ linux-amd64), Linux aarch64 (→ linux-arm64).

VERSION=v0.3.0 SYS=darwin-arm64
cd /tmp
curl -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$VERSION/zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS.tar.gz"
curl -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$VERSION/SHA256SUMS"
shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS      # Linux: sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS; must say OK
tar -xzf "zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS.tar.gz"
mkdir -p ~/bin && mv "zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS/zotero-backup" ~/bin/
~/bin/zotero-backup upgrade stable --yes          # to the newest normal release, if there is a newer one

Put ~/bin on the PATH, now and for every later login (Linux with bash: ~/.profile instead of ~/.zshrc), and check:

case ":$PATH:" in *":$HOME/bin:"*) ;; *) echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc; export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" ;; esac
zotero-backup version

A file downloaded with curl has no quarantine flag, so macOS does not block its first start.

Windows: the same in PowerShell (Over SSH has the commands; they work locally too).

With a browser instead: download the archive for your system from the releases, unpack it and put zotero-backup (zotero-backup.exe on Windows) somewhere on your PATH; on macOS the first start is then blocked once (below). Then zotero-backup upgrade stable.

Or build it with Go: go install github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup@latest (updated the same way, not with upgrade).

Later versions: zotero-backup upgrade stable (Updating). On another computer, from a terminal: Over SSH.

Windows and Linux: not yet tried on a real system

Only the macOS version has been checked by hand so far; the Windows and Linux versions pass the unit tests in CI but are untested in real use (#15, #16). See Platform status.

docs.title: macOS: the first start is blocked
docs.text:
zotero-backup is not signed and notarised by Apple, so macOS blocks a binary downloaded with a browser on its first start: a dialog says it was "Not Opened" because Apple could not check it for malicious software. Click Done (not "Move to Trash"), then either

  • open System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down to the message about zotero-backup and click Open Anyway; start it again and confirm with Open (with your password or Touch ID), or

  • remove the download's quarantine flag in Terminal, in the folder with the binary:

    xattr -d com.apple.quarantine zotero-backup

Either is needed once per downloaded binary. Archives downloaded with curl or gh release download carry no quarantine flag and start without this.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
From version 0.3.0 on, zotero-backup updates itself from the releases:

zotero-backup upgrade            # shows the newest stable and beta release, asks which
zotero-backup upgrade stable     # the newest normal release
zotero-backup upgrade beta       # the newest release, pre-releases included
zotero-backup upgrade --check    # only shows what there is (exit status 1: an update is available)
  • It shows the release page and asks before it changes anything; --yes skips the question (needed off a terminal, e.g. in scripts). It never runs on its own, and never during a backup or restore.
  • stable never goes back: on a pre-release it installs a stable release only once one is newer. To go back from a pre-release to the newest stable release: zotero-backup upgrade stable --downgrade.
  • Checked before anything is replaced: it downloads the archive for your system, SHA256SUMS and its signature, only from this repository's releases over HTTPS; checks the signature (Ed25519, the key is built into zotero-backup), then the archive's checksum; unpacks only the program next to the running one; and checks that the new file reports the expected version. Then it puts the new file in place of the old one. If anything fails, nothing is replaced and the release page is shown.
  • Where zotero-backup sits in a folder you cannot write to (e.g. /usr/local/bin), it says so: run it with sudo (Windows: as administrator).
  • On macOS, a program updated this way starts without the Gatekeeper question above (it was not downloaded by a browser).
  • Built with go install (version dev): update it with go install github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup@latest instead.

docs.title: API key
docs.text:
Create a key at https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys. For backups a read-only key is enough (personal library with notes and files, groups read). Restore needs a key with write access; keep that one for restores only.

The key is read from the environment variable ZOTERO_API_KEY, or else from the system keychain entry named by the profile's key (see Keys). It is never written to the configuration, the backups or the logs, and never taken as a command-line argument.

zotero-backup key check

shows the key's user and what it may do in each library.

docs.title: Two keys: one to back up, one to restore
docs.text:
Create two API keys at https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys (Create new private key), one for each job:

Key Settings at zotero.org Used by read-only, e.g. "zotero-backup read" Personal Library: Allow library access and Allow notes access, not Allow write access; Default Group Permissions: Read Only backup, list, diff, scheduled backups read/write, e.g. "zotero-backup restore" the same plus Allow write access; Default Group Permissions: Read/Write restore only

Store both on the computer you work and restore on, under two names, and tell the profile which is which:

zotero-backup key set                  # the read-only key, stored as "zotero-backup" (the profile's "key")
zotero-backup key set zotero-write     # the read/write key; then "write_key": "zotero-write" in the profile
zotero-backup key check                # both, and what each may do

Then backups, including scheduled ones, can never change a library, and restore uses the write key by itself. A computer that only makes backups (a server, a computer you reach over SSH) gets only the read-only key (Over SSH).

docs.title: Names and commands
docs.text:
Keys are stored in the system keychain under a name; the configuration only holds the name (the profile's key, default zotero-backup):

zotero-backup key set              # asks for the key (no echo), checks it with Zotero, stores it as "zotero-backup"
zotero-backup key set readonly     # …under another name; use it with "key": "readonly" in a profile
zotero-backup key check readonly   # user, libraries and rights of that key
zotero-backup key check            # every key the profile uses, and what each is for

A read-only key as key and a write key as write_key (see above) keep scheduled backups from ever changing a library, while restore uses the write key without further options:

zotero-backup key set zotero-write    # then "write_key": "zotero-write" in the profile
zotero-backup key remove readonly  # deletes the keychain entry (the key stays valid at zotero.org)

A key can also be piped in (… | zotero-backup key set), e.g. from a password manager.

System Keychain macOS Keychain (entry: service = name) Windows Credential Manager (generic credential, target = name) Linux desktop Secret Service: GNOME Keyring, KWallet, KeePassXC, through secret-tool (package libsecret-tools or libsecret) Linux server usually no keychain: set ZOTERO_API_KEY, e.g. from an encrypted systemd credential (see above)

ZOTERO_API_KEY always wins over the keychain.

docs.title: Off-site copies
docs.text:
Backups on one disk are lost with that disk (or the computer, or the house). Keep a second copy elsewhere: an external drive, a NAS, another computer.

The one thing to know: unchanged files are hard links between backups (Backups). A copy that does not keep them stores every file once per backup, so a folder of 30 backups needs about 30 times the space. Copy the whole backup folder (~/zotero-backups) at once, with a tool that keeps hard links.

docs.title: rsync (macOS, Linux)
docs.text:
rsync -aH --delete ~/zotero-backups/ /Volumes/BackupDisk/zotero-backups/
  • -a keeps dates and permissions, -H keeps the hard links, --delete removes backups that prune removed (leave it out to keep every backup on the copy).
  • The trailing / matters: it copies the folder's content, not the folder into itself.
  • To a NAS or another computer over SSH: rsync -aH --delete ~/zotero-backups/ me@nas:zotero-backups/.
  • Checked with the rsync that comes with macOS (openrsync, macOS 27), with rsync 3 (Homebrew) and with tar: all keep the links. Finder, cp -R and Windows Explorer do not.
  • Run it after the scheduled backup, e.g. as a second step of your own schedule, or by hand.

On Windows, robocopy does not keep hard links; copy from WSL with rsync -aH, or keep an archive (below).

docs.title: Archives
docs.text:
tar keeps hard links, so an archive is as small as the backup folder:

tar -czf zotero-backups-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C ~ zotero-backups

An archive is one file: it suits a cloud folder, a USB stick or a drive formatted FAT/exFAT (which knows no hard links).

docs.title: Backup software and cloud folders
docs.text:
• Time Machine and similar tools back up ~/zotero-backups like any other folder. Whether they keep the hard links depends on the tool: check the space the backups take there after a few runs.
  • Cloud folders (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive) store every hard link as a file of its own: do not put the backup folder into one. Put an archive there instead, or only the newest backup (zotero-backup list shows it).

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Backups contain your whole library: notes, PDFs, annotations. A copy that leaves the house belongs on an encrypted disk or volume: an encrypted APFS volume or disk image (Disk Utility) on macOS, BitLocker on Windows, LUKS on Linux, or an encrypted NAS share. zotero-backup does not encrypt itself.

docs.title: Checking a copy
docs.text:
• zotero-backup list and find work on a copy as well (--config with a profile whose to is the copy, or find TEXT LIBRARY_FOLDER with a library folder of the copy).
  • zotero-backup diff COPY ORIGINAL (two backup folders) compares the copy's metadata with the original's: "No differences." means the same items, collections, settings and file checksums. It does not read the files themselves; rsync -aHc --dry-run --itemize-changes SOURCE/ COPY/ lists files whose content differs. A full check of a backup's files is planned (#23).
  • Restoring from a copy works like from the original: restore reads only the backup folder you give it.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
Restore changes your library

Run diff and restore --dry-run first, and sync every Zotero app before restoring. You are responsible for the result: see the disclaimer.

zotero-backup diff BACKUP                     # what differs from the library today
zotero-backup diff BACKUP1 BACKUP2            # what changed between two backups (offline)
zotero-backup restore BACKUP --dry-run        # what restore would do
zotero-backup restore BACKUP                  # shows the plan, asks, restores, checks
zotero-backup restore BACKUP --items ABCD1234,EFGH5678
zotero-backup restore BACKUP --trash-new      # also move what is not in the backup to the trash
zotero-backup restore BACKUP --erase-new      # also erase what is not in the backup, for good

BACKUP is a backup folder, or a library folder for its newest backup. Restore writes into the same library the backup came from: missing items, collections and searches are recreated with their old keys, changed ones set back, items taken out of (or put back into) the trash, files uploaded (or attached again if Zotero still has them), tag colours set back. Items added since the backup are kept. --items restores only these items, with their children (attachments, notes, annotations), their parents and the collections they need. At the end the library is read again and compared with the backup.

docs.title: What restore changes and what it keeps
docs.text:
Restore never deletes anything that is not in the backup, unless asked to with --trash-new or --erase-new (below). Everything that is in the backup is set back to its state at the time of the backup.

Set back to the backup Kept as it is Items, collections and saved searches missing from the library: recreated with their old keys Items, notes, annotations, attachments, collections and saved searches created after the backup Objects changed since the backup: all fields, tags, collection memberships, note text; a field that was empty in the backup is cleared again The collection memberships of those new items (a new item in an old collection stays there) Trash state: items and collections put back into or taken out of the trash as they were; subcollections of a collection taken out of the trash are written once more, so that Zotero desktop takes them out of its trash too (Zotero desktop trashes them with their parent only locally) Files whose content differs from the backup: uploaded again Library settings, e.g. tag colours, as a whole: a tag colour assigned after the backup is removed

So changes made since the backup to anything that was in the backup are lost. The plan lists every object that will change before you confirm, and diff or --dry-run show it beforehand; objects that are only in the library are listed as "only in the library, not in the backup (restore keeps them)".

docs.title: Removing what is not in the backup
docs.text:
By default restore keeps everything created after the backup. To get the library back exactly as it was:

  • --trash-new also moves everything that is not in the backup to the Zotero trash: new items (their attachments, notes and annotations go with them), new notes, attachments and annotations under items that are in the backup, new collections and subcollections, new saved searches. From the trash they can be brought back, and citations of them in Word or Google Docs still work until the trash is emptied. What is already in the trash stays there.
  • --erase-new erases all of that for good, including what is not in the backup but already in the trash. Erased items cannot be brought back (only from another backup), their files are gone from the Zotero storage, and citations of them in documents no longer resolve.

Both are given on the command line each time (they cannot be set in the configuration), cannot be combined with --items, and show in the plan as their own section ("not in the backup: moved to the trash" or "ERASED FOR GOOD") with a count, and in the question. Run --dry-run with them first.

  • What a backup left out is never removed: a backup made with --exclude notes has no notes, so the library's notes do not count as "not in the backup" (the same for attachments, annotations and the trash).
  • Removing happens after everything in the backup was written back, so an object that had been moved under a new item or collection is back in place before that is removed. Erasing never takes an object that is in the backup with it.
  • As for any restore: sync every Zotero app first. An app with unsynced new items uploads them again afterwards.

docs.title: Selected items
docs.text:
With --items, only the chosen items change (with their children, parents and the collections they need); library settings are left alone.

Before a restore, sync every Zotero app that works on the library. If the restore changed an object that a Zotero app has unsynced changes to, that app shows the conflict window on its next sync (even when the two changes are in different fields), and whatever is chosen there wins over the restore. Unsynced changes to objects the restore did not change are uploaded as usual and stay. If that happened, run restore again; or, on that computer, use Zotero → Settings → Sync → Reset → Restore from Online Library (not "Replace Online Library", which goes the other way).

Restoring files counts against the library owner's Zotero storage.

docs.title: Scheduled backups
docs.text:
Run backup and then prune, e.g. daily. With no terminal, progress is written as plain lines every progress_interval seconds; use --quiet for only the summary and errors.

The computer has to be on and online at that time; Zotero desktop does not need to run (backups use the web API only). Use a read-only key for scheduled backups, so a key that is stored for unattended runs cannot change any library.

docs.title: The quick way
docs.text:
zotero-backup schedule install --at 02:30    # daily backup, then prune
zotero-backup schedule show                  # when, what it runs, log, state
zotero-backup schedule show raw              # the files themselves and the scheduler's own output
zotero-backup schedule remove

It sets up what the sections below describe, with your system's own scheduler, running while you are logged in: a LaunchAgent on macOS (~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.zotero-backup.plist, log ~/Library/Logs/zotero-backup.log), a systemd user timer on Linux (~/.config/systemd/user/zotero-backup.timer, log in the journal) or a scheduled task on Windows (log in %LOCALAPPDATA%\zotero-backup). The job runs backup and then prune with progress as log lines, using this program's full path; --profile and --config are passed on (another profile gets its own job, e.g. org.zotero-backup.work). Default time 06:00.

  • Store the key first (zotero-backup key set): the job reads it from your keychain.
  • It never overwrites or removes a setup it did not write itself (e.g. one copied from below by hand): it says so and stops.
  • Install zotero-backup in its final place first: the job keeps the path of the program it was set up with (upgrade replaces the file in place, so the job stays valid). install and show say so when that is not the zotero-backup on your PATH; running schedule install again with the right one replaces the job.
  • For runs while nobody is logged in, use the manual setups below.
  • A backup started by hand that still runs when the schedule comes up is safe: the scheduled run skips the libraries it is working on (Backups → One run per library). zotero-backup status shows what runs, zotero-backup stop stops it.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
The setups below run while you are logged in (a locked screen is fine). For runs when nobody is logged in, see below: the schedule is easy, the key is the point, because a keychain is only unlocked by logging in.

macOS (launchd): save as ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.zotero-backup.plist, then launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.zotero-backup.plist. Runs as you, so the keychain entry is available.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>org.zotero-backup</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>/bin/sh</string><string>-c</string>
    <string>/usr/local/bin/zotero-backup backup && /usr/local/bin/zotero-backup prune</string>
  </array>
  <key>StartCalendarInterval</key><dict><key>Hour</key><integer>6</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>0</integer></dict>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/tmp/zotero-backup.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/tmp/zotero-backup.log</string>
</dict></plist>

Linux (systemd timer, as your user): ~/.config/systemd/user/zotero-backup.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/zotero-backup backup
ExecStartPost=/usr/local/bin/zotero-backup prune
# On a server without a keychain, give the key as an encrypted systemd credential
# (user services need systemd 256 or newer and `systemd-creds --user`):
#   systemd-creds --user encrypt --name=zotero - ~/.config/zotero-backup/key.cred   (type the key, then Ctrl-D)
# LoadCredentialEncrypted=zotero:%h/.config/zotero-backup/key.cred
# ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'ZOTERO_API_KEY=$(cat "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/zotero") exec /usr/local/bin/zotero-backup backup'

and ~/.config/systemd/user/zotero-backup.timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

then systemctl --user enable --now zotero-backup.timer (and loginctl enable-linger $USER on a server, so it runs without a login). With cron instead: 0 6 * * * /usr/local/bin/zotero-backup backup --quiet && /usr/local/bin/zotero-backup prune.

Windows (Task Scheduler), in a command prompt:

schtasks /Create /SC DAILY /ST 06:00 /TN "zotero-backup" /TR "cmd /c \"C:\Tools\zotero-backup.exe backup && C:\Tools\zotero-backup.exe prune\""

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
A scheduled backup that fails says so only in its log. To hear about it, set in the profile (Configuration):

"notify_macos": true,
"notify_command": ["/usr/bin/mail", "-s", "zotero-backup failed", "me@example.org"]
  • Sent after a backup that failed (a library could not be backed up, no key, …) or reported problems in meta.json; not for attachments whose file never reached the server (missing_files), which are common.
  • notify_command is a program and its arguments, run without a shell, with the summary on stdin and ZB_STATUS (failed, problems) and ZB_LIBRARIES_FAILED in the environment; ZOTERO_API_KEY is removed from its environment. Any tool works: mail, curl to ntfy (["curl", "-T", "-", "https://ntfy.sh/my-topic"]), a script of your own.
  • notify_macos shows a macOS notification (Notification Center). Under a LaunchDaemon (nobody logged in) there is no one to show it to: use notify_command there.
  • A notification that fails is reported in the log and does not change the backup's result.
  • Try it: zotero-backup notify-test.

docs.title: When nobody is logged in
Another computer over SSH
docs.text:
Setting up zotero-backup on another computer from a terminal, over SSH: install, store the key, set up the daily backup. Written for an account that is logged in on that computer (at its screen, or with automatic login), e.g. a Mac mini with a server account that is always logged in. For a computer where nobody is logged in, see Scheduled backups → When nobody is logged in.

Log in over SSH as the account that will own the backups: the program, the key and the schedule all belong to that account.

ssh server@macmini.local

What has been tried

macOS: the whole workflow was set up over SSH on a Mac with an account that is always logged in (v0.3.0: install, security unlock-keychain and key set, first backup, schedule install). The Linux and Windows parts are written from how those systems work but not yet tried on a real system (#15 Windows, #16 Linux). Reports are welcome.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Install any release from v0.3.0 on (the first with upgrade), then let zotero-backup bring itself to the newest: the commands below stay the same for every future release, and the update is checked with zotero-backup's signature, not only a checksum.

Find out which archive fits: uname -sm prints e.g. Darwin arm64 (→ darwin-arm64), Darwin x86_64 (→ darwin-amd64), Linux x86_64 (→ linux-amd64), Linux aarch64 (→ linux-arm64). Then:

VERSION=v0.3.0 SYS=darwin-arm64
cd /tmp
curl -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$VERSION/zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS.tar.gz"
curl -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$VERSION/SHA256SUMS"
shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS      # Linux: sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf "zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS.tar.gz"
mkdir -p ~/bin && mv "zotero-backup-$VERSION-$SYS/zotero-backup" ~/bin/
~/bin/zotero-backup upgrade stable --yes       # to the newest normal release (signed), if there is a newer one

Put ~/bin on the PATH, now and for every later login (on Linux with bash use ~/.profile instead of ~/.zshrc):

case ":$PATH:" in *":$HOME/bin:"*) ;; *) echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc; export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" ;; esac
zotero-backup version

Windows (PowerShell over OpenSSH; curl.exe and tar come with Windows 10 and 11):

$V = "v0.3.0"; $S = "windows-amd64"
cd $env:TEMP
curl.exe -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$V/zotero-backup-$V-$S.zip"
curl.exe -LO "https://github.com/rkrug/zotero-backup/releases/download/$V/SHA256SUMS"
(Get-FileHash "zotero-backup-$V-$S.zip" -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower()   # must equal its line in SHA256SUMS
tar -xf "zotero-backup-$V-$S.zip"
mkdir -Force $HOME\bin; move "zotero-backup-$V-$S\zotero-backup.exe" $HOME\bin\
& $HOME\bin\zotero-backup.exe upgrade stable --yes
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$HOME\bin", "User")

(the Path change counts from the next login).

  • The checksum line must say OK for the archive.
  • zotero-backup version must work without the path in front; if it says "command not found", the PATH line is missing (echo $PATH). The schedule itself does not need it: it runs the program by its full path.
  • A file downloaded with curl has no quarantine flag: macOS does not block its first start (unlike a browser download, see Install).
  • upgrade stable says "is up to date on the stable channel" when the installed release already is the newest; later it fetches the newest and checks it before replacing anything (Updating). It replaces the file in place, so a schedule keeps working; run it the same way for every later update.

docs.title: 2. Store the key
docs.text:
Only a read-only key here

A computer you set up over SSH runs unattended, can be reached from elsewhere, and keeps its keychain unlocked for a long time. Store only a read-only key there: if the computer or its account is ever misused, the key can read your libraries but never change or delete anything in them. No write_key in its profile.

Create the read-only key at https://www.zotero.org/settings/keys: Allow library access and Allow notes access, not Allow write access, Default Group Permissions Read Only (Keys → Two keys). Keep the read/write key for restores on the computer you work on.

key set asks for the key without showing it; over SSH the typed key travels encrypted and never lands in a command line or the shell history. key check shows what the key may do: it must say read-only for every library.

macOS. The login keychain is unlocked while the account is logged in, but an SSH session often cannot use it until it is unlocked there too. Unlock it (it asks for the account's password), then store and check the key:

security unlock-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
zotero-backup key set
zotero-backup key check

Without the unlock, key set fails with a message like "User interaction is not allowed".

Linux. The keyring (GNOME Keyring, KWallet) belongs to the desktop session; an SSH session usually cannot reach it, even while you are logged in at the screen. Run key set in a terminal on the computer itself, or, on a server without a desktop, give the key as an encrypted systemd credential instead (Scheduled backups, the Linux service).

Windows (OpenSSH server, unchecked): zotero-backup key set stores the key in the Credential Manager of the SSH session's account. Windows may refuse that in an SSH session that logged in with an SSH key instead of the account's password; then log in with the password, or run key set at the computer.

docs.title: 3. A first backup
docs.text:
zotero-backup backup
zotero-backup list

The backups go to ~/zotero-backups of that account (zotero-backup config shows the folder; change it in the configuration). Before the first scheduled run, look at what prune would delete:

zotero-backup prune --dry-run

docs.title: 4. The daily backup
docs.text:
zotero-backup schedule install --at 02:30
zotero-backup schedule show

schedule show must name ~/bin/zotero-backup (the program you installed); if it says the job's program is not the zotero-backup on your PATH, run schedule install again with the right one (Scheduled backups → The quick way).

  • macOS: a LaunchAgent in the account's login session. Over SSH this works because the account is logged in at the screen; if it is not, launchctl refuses and the job cannot run.
  • Linux: a systemd user timer. It runs while the account has a session; for runs at night without one, loginctl enable-linger $USER (once, may need sudo). With the key as a systemd credential, use the service from Scheduled backups instead of schedule install.
  • Windows (unchecked): a scheduled task for the SSH session's account, which runs while that account is logged on.

Check the next day:

zotero-backup list
zotero-backup schedule show
tail -50 ~/Library/Logs/zotero-backup.log        # macOS; Linux: journalctl --user -u zotero-backup

To hear about failures without logging in: notify_command in the profile, e.g. mail or ntfy (Scheduled backups → Notifications).

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text: Restore on the computer you work on, with the read/write key stored there, from a copy of the server's backups (Off-site copies, e.g. rsync -aH server@macmini.local:zotero-backups/ ~/zotero-backups-server/): restore reads only the backup folder you give it. If a restore must run on the server itself, store the write key there only for that (zotero-backup key set zotero-write, then restore … --key zotero-write), remove it afterwards (zotero-backup key remove zotero-write), and delete that key at zotero.org.

docs.title: A computer that is always logged in
docs.text:
• The keychain must stay unlocked. By default the macOS login keychain does not lock on its own; if it is set to lock after some time or on sleep (Keychain Access → login keychain → Change Settings), scheduled runs fail with "no API key … the keychain could not be read". A notification tells you.
  • After a restart nothing runs until the account is logged in again: automatic login (System Settings → Users & Groups), and with FileVault on, someone must unlock the disk at the login screen first.
  • Sleep: a run missed while the computer slept follows when it wakes; for a server, turn off sleep or schedule a wake (System Settings → Energy).
  • Disk space: the backups grow with every changed file; prune keeps the newest of each of the last 7 days, 5 weeks and 12 months by default. A second copy elsewhere: Off-site copies.

docs.title: Stress test
docs.text:
zotero-backup stresstest checks that a restore holds up against what people actually do in Zotero: changes on another computer, unsynced work, deletions, the trash, and Zotero's conflict window. It runs 15 operations through 5 scenarios plus a set of extras, against the real Zotero server and a running Zotero desktop, and writes an HTML report to read and a JSON report for further processing.

The unit tests (go test ./..., run in CI on Linux, macOS and Windows) use a fake Zotero server and never involve the Zotero app. They cannot show how Zotero desktop reacts when a restore changes the server under it. The stress test does exactly that.

The stress test changes the libraries it runs on. Run it only on test groups or libraries. It is left out of zotero-backup help for that reason.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Recommended: a separate Zotero account just for testing. Create a second Zotero account, sign in to it in a separate Zotero profile with the Debug Bridge plugin, and create its API key there. Its personal library and any group it owns are then truly throw-away, and no key involved can reach your real libraries at all. With your normal account, a key that may write to the personal library can write to the whole of it, because an account has only one.

  • The write key must not reach anything else. Before asking, the test checks what the write key may do and refuses if --library is given and the key can write to any library not named there (the personal library or any group), listing them. Create the key at zotero.org/settings/keys with write access only to the test libraries; even a fault in the test then cannot change anything else on the server.
  • Only the libraries the write key may write to: all of them, or those named with --library group:<id> or --library user (the key's personal library). all is refused.
  • A question per library, before anything changes. After checking all libraries, it asks for each:
This test is altering the content of the group or library.
DO ONLY RUN IT ON A TEST GROUP OR LIBRARY!
Are you sure that the group "Safe Edit Test" (ID 6719916, 788 items on zotero.org; Zotero data folder …) is a test group or library, and you want to run the test there? [N/y]

The default is no. The question needs a terminal: a piped answer is refused, and there is no option to skip it. - Pinned to one library. Every script it runs inside Zotero first checks the library: a group by its ID and name, the personal library by the signed-in user's ID and username, which must be the key's. It stops on any mismatch. Syncs are limited to that library. - Only its own objects. Items count as the test's only if their top-level item carries the tag zb-e2e; collections only if their name starts with [zb-e2e]. Every operation refuses any other object. - Refuses to start on a library if the key cannot write to it, Zotero has unsynced changes in it, it was never synced, or automatic sync is on. - Safety backup first. Before anything changes in a library, a normal backup of it goes into the profile's backup folder (to). - Cleanup check at the end. For each library it erases what it created (by its run tag, collection names and tag colours), syncs, and compares the library with its safety backup: any difference is a failed check. - Keys are never shown. The API keys come from the keychain, the Debug Bridge token from the Zotero profile's prefs.js.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Part What Notes Zotero desktop running, signed in as the key's user automatic sync off; the libraries under test completely synced Zotero Debug Bridge plugin in that Zotero profile, with a token set the test runs JavaScript inside Zotero through it (POST 127.0.0.1:23119/debug-bridge/execute) Write key --key NAME, or the profile's write_key, else its key write access to every library under test, and to nothing else (checked) Read-only key the profile's key, if it cannot write only for the check that a read-only key is refused (skipped otherwise) Zotero profile --zotero-profile NAME\|FOLDER default: the default profile in Zotero's profiles.ini; ZOTERO_DEBUG_BRIDGE_TOKEN overrides the token

Safe Edit and Fix Proposals, if installed, are not used: neither intercepts how Zotero saves, so the test's script changes go past them, and their own changes wait for approval in a dialog.

Conflict window. When a sync finds an object changed on both sides, Zotero opens its conflict window and waits for a click. During the test's syncs, Zotero's function that opens it is temporarily replaced by one that answers "local" or "server" as the scenario requires, records every conflict it would have shown, and is put back right after the sync.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
zotero-backup stresstest without options shows these steps as help. Store the write key in the keychain, then run:

zotero-backup key set zb-test-write
zotero-backup stresstest --key zb-test-write --scenarios desktop-synced --ops edit-title,erase-item,replace-file
zotero-backup stresstest --key zb-test-write

No configuration file is needed: backups go to ~/zotero-backups, the test's own backups and reports into stresstest/<run>/ below it. A profile can hold the keys and the folder instead (--profile test):

{
  "profiles": {
    "test": {
      "key": "zb-test-read",
      "write_key": "zb-test-write",
      "to": "~/zotero-backups"
    }
  }
}

write_key is used for all changes; key, if it cannot write, only for the check that a read-only key is refused (skipped otherwise); to is the backup folder.

Option Default Meaning --key NAME the profile's keys keychain entry of the write key --library LIB every library the key may write to only group:<id> or user; repeat for several, run in that order --scenarios A,B all, plus extras which scenarios run --ops A,B all 15 which operations run --report DIR the run's backup folder where report.html and report.json go --keep off keep the test objects at the end, to look at them in Zotero (the cleanup check is skipped) --cleanup RUN only erase the test objects run RUN left behind and sync, e.g. after Zotero was closed during a run (RUN is the name of the run's report folder, e.g. 20261109T140228). Asks per library like a run --zotero-profile P the default profile the Zotero profile whose Debug Bridge token is used

The run's backups go to <to>/stresstest/<run>/; the safety backups to <to> like normal backups. The command fails (exit status 1) if any check failed.

Duration: not measured yet. Estimated 30–45 minutes for a group like Safe Edit Test (788 items); much longer for a library with thousands of items, since every backup and every comparison reads the whole library (about 15 times per scenario).

docs.title: Fixtures and operations
docs.text:
Every operation acts on its own fixture family, created fresh in Zotero desktop for each scenario, so all operations go through one backup and restore at once without getting in each other's way. A family is:

  • a book (title, date) with the tags zb-e2e, zb-e2e-run-<run>, zb-e2e-t1 and a coloured tag zb-e2e-colour-<run>-<op>
  • in a collection [zb-e2e] <run> <op> and its subcollection
  • a child note, a text attachment, and a PDF attachment with a highlight annotation

Each operation exists twice: done in Zotero desktop, and done directly on the server through the API, as another Zotero client would.

Operation What it does Touches edit-title changes the title item field fill-extra fills Extra, which is empty in the backup field absent from the backup trash-item moves the book to the trash trash erase-item erases the book with all children and files whole family erase-note erases the child note child item erase-attachment erases the PDF with its annotation attachment, file, annotation erase-annotation erases the annotation annotation edit-note adds a paragraph to the note note replace-file gives the text attachment new content file, md5 trash-collection moves the collection to the trash (Zotero 7) collection trash erase-collection erases the collection with its subcollection collections, memberships move-membership takes the book out of the collection, keeps the subcollection collection membership tags removes zb-e2e-t1, adds zb-e2e-added tags tag-colour changes the coloured tag's colour library setting tagColors new-item creates an item after the backup must be kept by restore

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Each scenario runs one cycle for all operations:

  1. Create the fixture families in Zotero desktop and sync them.
  2. Back up the library (backup B0).
  3. Make the changes as the scenario says; where desktop changes are synced, check that the server has them (and equals the desktop).
  4. Restore B0.
  5. Sync Zotero desktop, answering the conflict window as the scenario says.
  6. Check (next section); where the scenario expects the restore to be undone, restore again, sync, check again.
  7. Back up again (B1) and check that unchanged files are hard links to B0.
Scenario Before the restore Conflict window answered Expected desktop-synced change in Zotero desktop, synced (none expected) server and desktop back to B0, no conflict api change on the server by another client (none expected) server and desktop back to B0, no conflict unsynced-remote change in desktop, synced; then a second change in desktop, not synced (a line in Extra, a note paragraph or a title suffix on the first item of the family still there) server server and desktop back to B0. The conflict window comes only where the restore changed the object with the second change; where it did not (e.g. the restore brought back an erased note, but the second change is on the parent item), the second change is simply uploaded and stays: checked as "second change … uploaded" unsynced-local as unsynced-remote local the local version wins for the whole object and undoes the restore (recorded); a second restore and sync bring B0 back unsynced-only change in desktop, not synced at all (none expected) restore finds nothing to do; after the sync the server has the change; a second restore brings B0 back

Extras (--scenarios extras), once per library on two families of their own, plus one web page item for the zipped attachments:

  • restore --dry-run writes nothing: the library version stays the same.
  • restore --items restores only the selected item's family; the other stays changed.
  • A read-only key is refused before anything is written.
  • A second full restore right after the first finds nothing to do.
  • An interrupted backup (dropped connections simulated after 2 file downloads) fails, leaves a .partial folder, and the next run finishes and reuses the files already downloaded.
  • Zipped attachments (operation zip in the report): an HTML attachment with a second file (a stylesheet) in its folder, made in Zotero desktop, which uploads both as one ZIP.
    • The backup keeps that ZIP as <name>.zip, with "zip": true, the page's md5 and both files inside.
    • A copy of the backup with a changed page (under zip/upload in the run's folder) is restored: restore really uploads the ZIP (anything in a real backup came from the server, which then only answers "exists"); the next backup gets exactly that ZIP back; after a sync Zotero desktop has both files with the right md5 in its storage folder.
    • The same in the form backups made before v0.2.0 kept ZIPs in (under the file's own name, with the ZIP's own md5, no "zip"): recognised as a ZIP, no file difference to the library; with a changed page, restore uploads it as a ZIP and the server has the page's md5.
  • Removing what is not in the backup (operation remove-new): after a backup, a new item with a child note, a note under a fixture item and a collection with a subcollection are made through the API; restore --trash-new puts them in the trash (the child note with its item) on the server and, after a sync, in Zotero desktop; restore --erase-new then erases them there too. Before each restore the plan is checked to remove only this test's own objects (tag zb-e2e, collections [zb-e2e]…); otherwise the step is refused.
  • prune --dry-run with one daily backup kept lists all but the newest backup.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
After each restore and sync, every fixture family is checked on its own:

Check Compares Passes when Backup has the fixture B0 all items, both collections and both files are in it Server has the change server vs B0, after the desktop's changes are synced and before the restore something differs: the change reached the server, so the restore has something to undo Server = backup server vs B0, with the comparison diff uses, plus the tag colour nothing differs (or, where the scenario expects it, something does) Desktop = server Zotero desktop vs server: fields, trash state, collections, file md5, tag colour nothing differs New items kept the item made after the backup still on the server, not in the trash Nothing left unsynced Zotero desktop after each sync 0 unsynced items and collections Hard links files in B1 vs B0 unchanged files are the same file on disk Cleanup each library vs its safety backup identical after the fixtures are erased

Files the server has newer than the desktop (put back by a restore) are downloaded before their md5 is compared.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
• report.html: summary (checks, passed, failed, observations), the libraries with their safety backups, the failed checks first, the scenarios, then every check.
  • report.json: the same for further processing:
{
  "run": "20261109T120000", "tool_version": "v0.1.0", "system": "darwin/arm64",
  "started": "…", "finished": "…", "backups": "~/zotero-backups/stresstest/20261109T120000",
  "libraries": [{"id": "group-6719916", "name": "Safe Edit Test", "safety_backup": "…"}],
  "scenarios_selected": null, "operations_selected": null,
  "summary": {"checks": 412, "passed": 410, "failed": 2, "observations": 9},
  "scenarios": [{"name": "api", "sequence": "…", "expected": "…"}],
  "results": [{"library": "group-6719916", "scenario": "api", "operation": "erase-item",
               "check": "after restore: server = backup", "result": "pass", "detail": "", "time": "…"}]
}

result is pass, fail or info (an observation, e.g. which conflicts Zotero's window would have shown, or that the local version won).

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• Changes through Safe Edit or Fix Proposals: both need approval in a dialog.
  • Other Zotero apps on other computers: the second client is simulated through the API.
  • Group renames and very large libraries: covered by earlier real runs (IPBES LDR, 6,975 items, 3.9 GB).
